title: FIREQ: FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control
authors: Giuseppe La Capra, Fabio Calabrese, Giorgio D'Amico, Christian Conti, Andrea De Simone, Deborah Volpe, Roldolfo Carobene, Claudio Gatti, Andrea Giachero, Fabrizio Riente
abstract: We present FIREQ (FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control), an open-source RFSoC-based framework for the control and readout of superconducting qubits. FIREQ combines a modular AXI-compliant firmware architecture with a PYNQ-based software stack designed to support extensible hardware integration, deterministic experiment timing, and low-overhead execution of repeated calibration and characterization workflows. The firmware implements direct RF synthesis and acquisition, trigger-based sequencing, programmable pulse generation, frequency-multiplexed readout, and memory-efficient acquisition and waveform buffering. The software adopts a client-server architecture with streamed data transfer and dependency-aware configuration updates to reduce host-device and reconfiguration overhead during parameter sweeps. On an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC ZCU216, FIREQ generates RF pulses up to 9.3 GHz with a pulse-duration resolution of 107 ps and an event-timing resolution of 1.7 ns. FPGA resource utilization is compared with representative open-source RFSoC control frameworks, showing a low BRAM footprint while retaining full-rate I/Q generation and acquisition. The RF output is characterized in terms of phase noise, noise spectral density, and inter-channel timing skew. End-to-end operation is validated on a superconducting qubit through resonator spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, and relaxation measurements, yielding T1 = 6.94 us and T2* = 13.50 us. FIREQ can therefore be used both as a qubit-control platform and as an experimental environment for evaluating alternative control and readout IP architectures.
summary: This paper presents FIREQ, an open-source, FPGA-based framework designed to overcome the scaling limitations of classical control electronics for superconducting qubits. By integrating all control and readout functions onto an RFSoC, it achieves high performance metrics, validating its use as a robust, modular platform for quantum experiments.
main_problem: The classical infrastructure required to control and measure superconducting qubits becomes a significant bottleneck as qubit counts scale.
main_result: The FIREQ framework successfully demonstrated end-to-end operation on a superconducting qubit, achieving T1 = 6.94 us and T2* = 13.50 us while maintaining low timing skew.
method: The authors developed an open-source, RFSoC-based hardware/software co-design framework that integrates RF synthesis, pulse generation, and readout directly onto an FPGA.
model_or_system: The system targets superconducting qubits, whose quantum state is modeled on the Bloch sphere and controlled via microwave pulses inducing rotations. The platform uses an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC for high-speed, deterministic control.
key_observables: Qubit coherence times ($T_1, T_2^*$), RF output phase noise, timing skew, and gate fidelity.
important_parameters: RF pulse generation up to 9.3 GHz with 107 ps resolution; $T_1 = 6.94 \mu	ext{s}$ and $T_2^* = 13.50 \mu	ext{s}$.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that integrating control/readout functions onto an RFSoC significantly reduces latency and overhead compared to conventional external instrumentation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system overview across cryogenic stages, the Bloch sphere representation of the qubit state, and detailed results from qubit characterization experiments (e.g., Rabi oscillations, $T_1$ measurements).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the hardware challenge, details the FIREQ architecture (firmware/software stack), validates the system performance metrics (timing skew, RF characterization), and concludes with experimental results on qubit spectroscopy and coherence measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, high-performance hardware platform for quantum control, which is crucial for experimentalists developing and testing new quantum algorithms or characterizing novel qubit modalities.
